question: Can one Lie-derivative formalism characterize when a model is equivariant, recover its continuous symmetry subgroup, and encourage a learned model to acquire a large subgroup of a user-specified candidate Lie group?

key_findings.claim: The framework reduces exact equivariance under a Lie group to linear infinitesimal and disconnected-component conditions on the learned section.
key_findings.evidence: For the induced action K_g F = Theta_(g^-1) composed with F composed with theta_g, the Lie derivative L_xi F is bilinear in the generator xi and section F. Vanishing L_xi F for a Lie-algebra generating set enforces equivariance under the identity component; one finite equality K_g F = F for a representative of every remaining connected component completes the full-group condition.

key_findings.claim: For a fixed section, continuous symmetry discovery becomes a nullspace problem, but the result identifies only the Lie algebra of the identity component.
key_findings.evidence: The symmetry transformations form a closed embedded Lie subgroup, and its Lie algebra is exactly Null(L_F), where L_F maps xi to L_xi F. The finite-sample proposition states almost-sure eventual recovery under exact tangent projections and independently sampled points of strictly positive measure, without a computable stopping threshold or a noisy-data guarantee.

key_findings.claim: The rank of the Lie-derivative operator measures continuous symmetry codimension, while its nuclear norm is a convex heuristic rather than an exact symmetry-recovery objective.
key_findings.evidence: Rank(L_F) equals the candidate Lie-algebra dimension minus the discovered symmetry dimension, so minimizing rank would maximize continuous symmetry. Because F maps linearly to L_F, the nuclear norm is convex in F and is proposed as a tractable surrogate. The paper proves neither that nuclear-norm minimization creates exact zero singular values nor that it recovers the maximally symmetric interpolant in this setting.

key_findings.claim: The abstract construction covers nonlinear base-space actions, vector and tensor fields, submanifold tangency, dynamical systems, Hamiltonian constraints, and integral operators, but most of this breadth is theorem-level rather than empirically demonstrated.
key_findings.evidence: Sections 11-17 lift the operators to vector bundles and derive symmetry or tangency conditions for sections, dynamics, Hamiltonians, conservation laws, and multilinear integral operators. The experiments, however, use polynomial functions and finite-dimensional ODE models; the conclusion explicitly leaves general vector-bundle empirical validation to future work.

key_findings.claim: The polynomial interpolation studies show that nuclear-norm minimization can select exactly symmetric coefficient tensors from fewer noiseless samples than generic unregularized interpolation requires.
key_findings.evidence: Across radial-polynomial and linear-feature families, ten random trials per configuration are summarized by mean curves and min-max shading. Recovery is declared when every coefficient is within 5e-3 times the largest true coefficient. The black-dot reference is the number of coefficients needed for generic exact interpolation, not a matched regularized learning or symmetry-discovery method, and neither observation noise nor candidate-group misspecification is tested.

key_findings.claim: The spring-mass example demonstrates qualitative out-of-plane extrapolation after symmetry promotion, but it is a single synthetic construction with no repeated held-out statistic.
key_findings.evidence: A five-particle system is trained on 100 state-derivative pairs from two trajectories restricted to the x-z plane. The SE(3)-candidate penalty recovers a vector field whose displayed test trajectory and coefficient matrices resemble ground truth, whereas sparse SINDy fails in the unseen y dynamics. Gamma is chosen as the largest value keeping training MSE below 1e-4; the paper reports no seeds, uncertainty, or numeric test table.

key_findings.claim: Equivariance-promoting neural networks improve low-data double-pendulum forecasts, but the experiment does not isolate the symmetry penalty from the proposed architecture.
key_findings.evidence: Twenty random experiments are run at each of M = 500, 250, 100, 50, 25, and 10 trajectory chunks. Smaller correct candidate groups generally yield the lowest low-data errors, yet even the EPNN with no symmetry penalty strongly outperforms the parameter-matched MLP when data are scarce. The EPNN and MLP use different block structures and activations, and no exactly equivariant EMLP baseline is included.

key_findings.claim: The EPNN penalty is convex in a layer's weights, but training the composed neural ODE remains nonconvex and depends on candidate representations assigned to every hidden space.
key_findings.evidence: The equivariance-promoting block multiplies an affine map by a sigmoid of a quadratic polynomial, and the discretized Lie-derivative entries are linear in the layer parameters. This makes the nuclear norm convex as a function of one layer's weights, not the end-to-end trajectory loss. Moreover, enforcing a common layerwise subgroup can exclude symmetries that arise only after layer composition or cancellation.

key_findings.claim: Finite sampling can exactly represent the relevant inner products for finite-dimensional model classes, but this does not establish robust empirical symmetry discovery from noisy observations.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 17 guarantees that sufficiently many samples eventually produce a valid discrete inner product, and Proposition 18 gives an almost-everywhere polynomial sampling bound based on coordinate projection dimensions. Both concern exact finite-dimensional function representations; they do not quantify estimation error, conditioning, sample complexity under noise, or model misspecification.

key_findings.claim: The supplied repository supports inspection of the polynomial experiments but does not reproduce the two dynamical-system studies or provide a working package installation.
key_findings.evidence: At audited commit 038f83eb647402bbb1f1ed7c4f2347110c9e41fa, the repository contains 12 Python files, three polynomial-result CSV files, and generic symmetry-layer code, but no spring-mass or double-pendulum training scripts, result tables, checkpoints, tests, CI, or pinned environment. setup.py filters discovered packages to names beginning with 'src' and then drops the first match; the actual symm_ml packages do not match, so the declared package list is empty. The CSVs contain exactly ten rows per polynomial configuration and align with Figures 5-7.

key_findings.claim: The method requires the user to choose a candidate group that contains the desired symmetry and is computationally small enough to discretize.
key_findings.evidence: The authors recommend the smallest plausible supergroup because the Lie-derivative tensor scales with candidate Lie-algebra dimension, model dimension, and discretization size. Their largest reported polynomial operator is 496 by 496 by 465 and takes about 40 CPU minutes, while they identify sparse, Krylov, randomized, and sketching methods as future work.

key_findings.claim: The core equivalences do not cover partial transformations, nonlinear fiber actions, or disconnected symmetry discovery without additional machinery.
key_findings.evidence: Lie-algebra nullspaces describe continuous identity components; separate finite representatives are required to enforce disconnected components. The paper states that partial symmetries cannot in general be captured by a Lie algebra, and its convexity uses fiber-linearity: a nonlinear action on outputs makes the induced Lie derivative nonlinear in F.

method.core_idea: Represent equivariance by the Lie derivative of a learned section under a candidate Lie-group action, then use the same bilinear operator for exact constraints, nullspace-based discovery, and rank-surrogate regularization.
method.mechanism: A group action on the input base and a fiber-linear action on outputs induce K_g on sections. Differentiating K along Lie-algebra directions produces L_xi F. Setting generator derivatives to zero enforces the connected group; taking Null(L_F) discovers the continuous symmetry algebra; penalizing the nuclear norm of L_F encourages a large nullspace. Discrete component defects are added separately, and sampled inner products turn the operators into matrices or tensors for optimization.
assumptions: The candidate transformation family is a finite-dimensional Lie group and the true connected symmetry is a subgroup of it.
Base actions and sections are sufficiently smooth for the induced infinitesimal derivatives and geometric theorems.
Fiber actions are linear when bilinearity and convexity in the learned section are required.
The chosen finite-dimensional function class and sampled inner products faithfully represent the continuous operators.
Exact nullspaces and rank are meaningful; the main discovery theory does not model observation noise or approximate symmetry.
Disconnected components are known well enough to supply one representative from each relevant component.
A sufficiently small candidate group and tractable discretization are available, and the architecture can express nontrivial equivariant functions.
Nuclear norm is an adequate proxy for symmetry dimension despite having no problem-specific exact-recovery theorem.

techniques.role: Converts actions on inputs and fibers into a transformation of learned sections whose fixed points are equivariant maps.
Differentiates the induced action to obtain infinitesimal constraints bilinear in group generators and model functions.
Recovers the Lie algebra of the model's connected symmetry subgroup as the kernel of the section-conditioned operator.
Uses a convex surrogate for operator rank to encourage more zero symmetry-breaking directions.
Adds finite transformation equalities for disconnected parts not visible to the Lie algebra.
Replaces continuous function-space inner products by finite evaluations, producing matrices and tensors for computation.
Builds layerwise symmetry-promoting networks from affine maps gated by sigmoid-transformed quadratic polynomials.
Extends symmetry tests to embedded submanifolds by relating Lie derivatives to normal components of induced vector fields.

evaluations.setting: Noiseless random radial-polynomial and linear-feature interpolation over varied ambient dimension, feature count, degree, and symmetry group, with ten seeds per configuration.
evaluations.metric: Fraction of recovered coefficient tensors satisfying a maximum coefficient error below 5e-3 times the largest true coefficient, summarized by mean and min-max sample thresholds.
evaluations.result: The nuclear-norm solution generally recovers the symmetric target below the generic coefficient-count threshold, with the largest relative savings for higher-dimensional or more strongly constrained cases.
evaluations.baseline: Exact unregularized interpolation at the number of free polynomial coefficients; no ridge, sparse, data-augmentation, or learned-symmetry baseline.

evaluations.setting: A five-particle spring-mass system with gravity, trained from two trajectories and 100 derivative samples confined to the x-z plane.
evaluations.metric: Training MSE threshold, learned coefficient heatmaps, and qualitative held-out trajectory coordinates outside the training plane.
evaluations.result: The largest SE(3)-candidate penalty retaining training MSE below 1e-4 produces matrices and a test trajectory visually close to ground truth; sparse SINDy does not recover the unseen y dynamics.
evaluations.baseline: L1-regularized SINDy and unregularized regression; one synthetic system with no repeated quantitative test statistic.

evaluations.setting: Twelve-dimensional double-spring-pendulum Neural ODE learning from M = 500, 250, 100, 50, 25, or 10 five-step trajectory chunks, with 20 random experiments at each size.
evaluations.metric: Boxplots of one-second chunk prediction error and 30-second trajectory error.
evaluations.result: EPNNs with smaller correct candidate groups have the best low-data medians, while broad candidates become less reliable at M = 10; the unpenalized EPNN also substantially beats the MLP in the low-data regime.
evaluations.baseline: A parameter-matched Swish MLP and an EPNN with no penalty; no exact EMLP, data-augmentation, Augerino, LieGAN, or relaxed-equivariance baseline.

evaluations.setting: Runtime examples for discretized polynomial Lie-derivative tensors.
evaluations.metric: Operator dimensions and CPU wall-clock time reported by the authors.
evaluations.result: An SE(30) tensor of size 496 by 496 by 465 takes about 40 CPU minutes; a translation example at n = 50 with size 1326 by 51 by 50 takes under one minute.
evaluations.baseline: Dense current implementation only; no sparse, low-rank, Krylov, GPU, or memory benchmark.

evaluations.setting: Public artifact audit at Git commit 038f83eb647402bbb1f1ed7c4f2347110c9e41fa.
evaluations.metric: Presence of scripts, result data, experiment coverage, tests, dependency locking, and installability.
evaluations.result: Polynomial scripts and 1,680 CSV result rows are present, but both dynamical experiments, outputs, tests, CI, and pinned dependencies are absent; setup.py declares no packages because its package-name filter excludes symm_ml.
evaluations.baseline: The canonical paper's three empirical sections and its README installation instruction.

limitations: Author-stated: the user must posit a candidate group containing the desired symmetries, and computational cost favors the smallest plausible group.
Author-stated: dense discretized Lie-derivative operators can be expensive; sparse, Krylov, randomized, and sketching algorithms remain future work.
Author-stated: the chosen function class or architecture must contain nontrivial functions with the sought symmetry.
Author-stated: partial symmetries are not generally captured by a Lie algebra, and general vector-bundle applications are not empirically tested.
Reviewer-identified: nuclear norm is only a rank surrogate; no theorem connects its minimizer to maximal exact symmetry or target recovery for these learning problems.

Reviewer-identified: the nullspace discovery guarantee is exact and asymptotic with an unknown sample threshold; it supplies no noisy estimator, confidence interval, conditioning analysis, or stopping rule.

Reviewer-identified: only identity-component symmetries are discovered automatically; disconnected symmetries require known representatives and partial or bounded transformations fall outside the formalism.
Reviewer-identified: penalty magnitude depends on the inner products, bases, sampling, and scale of the induced operator, complicating cross-group and cross-layer regularization.

Reviewer-identified: all empirical tasks are synthetic, and the polynomial study uses noiseless exact interpolation against a coefficient-count reference rather than strong symmetry-learning baselines.
Reviewer-identified: the spring result has no repetitions or numeric held-out summary, and gamma is selected by training rather than validation error.

Reviewer-identified: EPNN versus MLP comparisons confound the regularizer with architecture and activation, while group-specific gamma values differ by four orders of magnitude without a common selection protocol.
Reviewer-identified: EPNN layerwise subgroup constraints can miss symmetries that emerge only from end-to-end composition.
Reviewer-identified: the artifact omits two of three experiment pipelines, has no tests or locked environment, and its packaging configuration makes the documented editable installation incomplete.

Reviewer-identified: the final source's Appendix F proof of the Lie-bracket relation repeats xi_1 in [theta-hat(xi_1), theta-hat(xi_1)] where the standard identity and surrounding derivation require xi_2 in the second argument.
failure_modes: If the true symmetry is outside the candidate group, the method can only enforce, discover, or promote its intersection with the supplied action family.
If the candidate group is too broad, dense operator construction becomes expensive and nuclear-norm optimization may be poorly scaled or ill-conditioned.
Approximate, noisy, local, state-dependent, or partial symmetries may produce small singular values without an identifiable exact nullspace.
Nonlinear fiber actions destroy linearity in the learned section and therefore the stated convex promotion mechanism.
Finite samples concentrated on a restricted set can introduce spurious infinitesimal null directions before the unknown exact-recovery threshold is reached.

Nuclear-norm shrinkage can reduce all singular values without making any direction exactly symmetric, or prefer a low-amplitude model rather than a task-useful symmetric one unless the task constraint is sufficiently strong.
Layerwise EPNN penalties can overconstrain a network when the end-to-end function has symmetries not shared by every intermediate representation.
Disconnected, reflection-like, or finite symmetries remain invisible unless their component representatives are explicitly supplied.
In very low data, an overly large candidate group can encourage a wrong high-symmetry solution or yield unstable training, as suggested by broad-group EPNN outliers at M = 10.
reusable_insights: Differentiate a global transformation law to obtain local linear constraints that are cheaper to check and can share one operator across enforcement and discovery.
The nullspace of a model-conditioned infinitesimal operator identifies continuous symmetries, while its rank measures how many candidate directions the model breaks.
Separate connected and disconnected symmetry handling: generators suffice for the identity component, but finite component representatives carry independent information.
Rank-promoting regularizers should be paired with explicit normalization and post-training singular-spectrum diagnostics because nuclear norm alone does not guarantee exact nullity.

A restricted-support training set can become informative when structural regularization couples unseen directions to observed ones, but extrapolation should be evaluated over repeated systems and perturbations.

Candidate-group size is a bias-computation tradeoff: smaller plausible supergroups reduce cost and can improve low-data accuracy, whereas broad groups express more hypotheses but weaken identifiability.
Geometric tangency constraints can be encoded as symmetry nullspaces, linking equivariance tools to invariant-manifold and conservation-law learning.
open_questions: Under what restricted-isometry, incoherence, or identifiability conditions does nuclear-norm minimization recover a maximally symmetric model rather than merely shrink the Lie-derivative spectrum?
How should the operator and penalty be normalized so gamma values are comparable across candidate groups, representations, layers, and sampled inner products?
Can noisy finite-sample symmetry discovery provide confidence sets for subgroup dimension and generators, rather than an exact eventual-nullspace statement?
How can disconnected, partial, local, or state-dependent symmetries be discovered rather than supplied in advance?
Do EPNN gains remain after matching nonlinearities and architecture and comparing with exact EMLPs, augmentation learning, LieGAN, LieSD, and relaxed-equivariant networks?
Can sparse or matrix-free operator methods make high-dimensional candidate groups practical without changing the recovered nullspace?
How robust is symmetry promotion to wrong candidate actions, weakly broken physical symmetries, observation noise, and real data?
Can end-to-end symmetry promotion avoid constraining each layer while retaining a computationally tractable operator?
Will the missing spring and pendulum pipelines, seeds, exact result arrays, and a corrected package configuration be released for full reproduction?

competitive_landscape.title: A Practical Method for Constructing Equivariant Multilayer Perceptrons for Arbitrary Matrix Groups
competitive_landscape.difference: Finzi, Welling, and Wilson solve linear nullspace constraints to construct exact equivariant MLP layers for arbitrary matrix groups. The reviewed work derives those constraints from a broader induced Lie derivative, extends them to nonlinear base actions and vector bundles, and adds discovery and rank-surrogate promotion, but does not empirically compare its EPNN with EMLP.

competitive_landscape.title: The Lie Derivative for Measuring Learned Equivariance
competitive_landscape.difference: Gruver et al. use Lie derivatives to measure local equivariance error for specified one-parameter transformations in trained models. The reviewed paper turns the generator-to-derivative map into a full candidate-algebra nullspace for subgroup discovery and a nuclear-norm training penalty, while requiring a prescribed finite-dimensional candidate action.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Invariances in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Augerino learns continuous augmentation ranges jointly with a predictor and can represent bounded partial invariances. The reviewed method instead promotes a lower-dimensional connected subgroup through an architectural Lie-derivative operator and has exact group-theoretic characterizations, but explicitly does not cover partial symmetries.

competitive_landscape.title: Approximately Equivariant Networks for Imperfectly Symmetric Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. relax equivariant layers to model imperfectly symmetric dynamics and test approximate symmetry breaking. The reviewed work supplies a more general candidate-subgroup and vector-bundle formalism with a convex layer penalty, but its theory targets exact subgroups and its experiments omit noisy or naturally broken symmetries.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Adversarial Symmetry Discovery
competitive_landscape.difference: LieGAN learns infinitesimal generators adversarially from a data distribution and demonstrates empirical continuous-symmetry discovery. The reviewed method obtains the exact symmetry algebra of a specified learned function by linear nullspace computation inside a supplied candidate representation, giving cleaner structure but a narrower discovery search and no discovery experiment.

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering Symmetry Breaking in Physical Systems with Relaxed Group Convolution
competitive_landscape.difference: Relaxed group convolution learns interpretable deviations from a highest-symmetry convolutional model and evaluates crystals, turbulence, and pendula. The reviewed work, submitted one month later, offers a broader operator-level treatment for arbitrary supplied Lie-group actions and subgroup promotion, but a substantially narrower synthetic empirical audit.

competitive_landscape.title: Symmetry Discovery for Different Data Types
competitive_landscape.difference: LieSD estimates Lie-algebra bases from inputs, outputs, and gradients for multiple data types and empirically recovers symmetry dimensions under varied sampling distributions. The reviewed framework is geometrically broader and uniquely integrates promotion, yet its nullspace discovery theory is not itself empirically evaluated.

competitive_landscape.title: Continuous Symmetry Discovery and Enforcement Using Infinitesimal Generators of Multi-parameter Group Actions
competitive_landscape.difference: Shaw et al. learn nonlinear vector-field generators of multi-parameter actions, automatically estimate their number, and enforce them with metric-aware regularization in empirical tasks. The reviewed work already permits nonlinear base actions abstractly and offers closed-subgroup theorems, but fixes a finite-dimensional candidate group and does not empirically discover nonlinear generators.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents a unified geometric framework in which the same Lie derivative enforces, discovers, and promotes symmetry for functions, vector-bundle sections, submanifolds, dynamics, Hamiltonian systems, and integral operators, and introduces nuclear-norm symmetry promotion and EPNNs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Theorems 3-4, 10, 25-26, 35, and 39 connect exact equivariance, closed symmetry subgroups, nullspaces, and tangency; Sections 7-8 define the rank/nuclear-norm objective and EPNN architecture; Sections 11-17 instantiate the common construction across geometric objects.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is the unusually broad operator-level synthesis and the observation that symmetry dimension is the nullity of an operator linear in both generators and the model, enabling a convex layerwise rank surrogate. Exact equivariant nullspace layers, Lie-derivative measurement, learned augmentation ranges, approximate equivariance, and adversarial symmetry discovery all predate it, while concurrent relaxed group convolutions already learn symmetry breaking empirically. Its strongest originality is therefore formal unification and subgroup-promotion machinery, not the first use of infinitesimal generators or the first learned-symmetry system; the empirical claim should remain narrow because baselines are weak or confounded and most geometric extensions are untested.

reviewer_notes: Reviewed the exact 72-page arXiv v3 PDF end to end, including every equation, theorem, proof appendix, reference, figure, table, caption, and the raster rendering of all pages. The indexed PDF hash and extracted-text hash match the source provenance. The TeX source archive (SHA-256 0ed1b57987a2589cbe1a864ce99f6b5d96ce18c2f28b4cedcc54c1e81d84e187) was audited, including 37 figure assets; it contains no experimental arrays or training code. The public repository was audited at commit 038f83eb647402bbb1f1ed7c4f2347110c9e41fa and its Python files compile, but its result and reproducibility omissions are recorded above. Primary arXiv records across Lie-derivative measurement, exact equivariant networks, learned augmentations, approximate equivariance, adversarial discovery, relaxed group convolution, and later generator discovery were checked at their current revisions on 2026-08-24. Author-reported statements are separated from reviewer inference and contradiction audits. The Appendix F repeated-generator typo is a local transcription error in a standard Lie-bracket proof, not evidence against the theorem. This is a primary full-text review, not an independent secondary verification.
